L0: 
L1: URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4329923/
L2: Editorial Commentary: Microbiologic Testing in Post–Solid Organ Transplant 
L3: Diarrhea \---------------------------------------- (See the Major Article by 
L4: Echenique et al on pages 729–37.) Up to 27% of recipients of solid organ 
L5: transplant (SOT) experience diarrhea posttransplant, with some episodes being 
L6: severe enough to require hospitalization [1–3]. Immunosuppressive medications 
L7: are a common cause, but reduction of immunosuppression carries the risk of 
L8: allograft rejection, making it necessary to rule out other causes, such as 
L9: infection, before modifying the immunosuppressive regimen [3–7]. In this issue 
L10: of Clinical Infectious Diseases, Echenique and colleagues report the frequency 
L11: of infectious causes and diagnostic yield of microbiologic tests in a large 
L12: retrospective cohort of hospitalized SOT patients with community- and hospital-
L13: onset diarrhea [8]. An implied goal of the study was to determine if a targeted 
L14: approach to testing for infectious causes of diarrhea could be considered as an 
L15: alternative to the more comprehensive testing strategies recommended at their 
L16: facility and elsewhere [7, 8]. With this question in mind, it is striking that 
L17: most diarrheal episodes in their study had no specific etiology identified, 
L18: infectious or otherwise, and >90% resolved in the hospital before discharge. A 
L19: potential infectious cause was identified in 30% of community-onset and 19% of 
L20: hospital-onset diarrheal episodes overall. Most infections were limited to just 
L21: 3 agents—Clostridium difficile, norovirus, or cytomegalovirus—which comprised 
L22: >90% of the infectious cases identified. Other infectious causes of diarrhea, 
L23: such as Campylobacter, Salmonella, rotavirus, adenovirus, astrovirus, 
L24: Cryptosporidium, and Giardia, were rarely identified. In light of these 
L25: findings, the authors suggest that initial testing for infectious causes of 
L26: diarrhea in SOT recipients could potentially be limited to a few tests (eg, 
L27: blood quantitative cytomegalovirus polymerase chain reaction [PCR], C. difficile
L28:  PCR, norovirus reverse transcription PCR, bacterial stool culture) in most 
L29: patients. Then, if symptoms persist, additional testing could be performed to 
L30: diagnose or rule out less common infectious causes before modifying 
L31: immunosuppressive regimens. An analogous tiered approach to testing has been 
L32: used for decades in immunocompetent patients with diarrhea. However, there are 
L33: several important points that should be considered before generalizing the 
L34: results of this study to other centers. First, the frequencies of several 
L35: potentially significant pathogens in immunocompromised hosts, such as 
L36: Campylobacter and Cryptosporidium, were lower in this study than previous 
L37: studies based in Europe (Table 1). Conversely, the rate of C. difficile among 
L38: community-onset diarrheal episodes was higher than other studies and comparable 
L39: to the rate of C. difficile in hospital-onset diarrheal episodes. This may be a 
L40: manifestation of the changing epidemiology of C. difficile with more 
L41: transmission and infection in the community or simply due to community onset of 
L42: symptoms after hospitalization [11, 12]. Alternatively, it is possible that some
L43:  of the C. difficile identified in community-onset diarrheal episodes were 
L44: recurrent infections or lingering colonization with another cause of symptoms, 
L45: as many patients had a history of prior C. difficile infection. In any case, the
L46:  differences in the rates of individual diarrheal pathogens in this study vs 
L47: previous studies suggests that the etiologies of infectious diarrhea in SOT 
L48: recipients likely differ between transplant centers. Hence, the authors note in 
L49: their discussion that the results of this study should not be generalized 
L50: without verification of the local epidemiology and validation. Table 1. 
L51: Frequency of Infectious Causes in Patients With Posttransplant Diarrhea, by 
L52: Study Study Echenique, 2014 (This Issue) [8] Maes et al, 2006 [7] Roos-Weil et 
L53: al, 2011 [9] Coste et al, 2013 [10] \----------------------------------------

L10: 26 July 2021 / Accepted: 5 August 2021 / Published: 12 August 2021 Abstract 
L11: Urinary tract infection (UTI) represents the most common infection after kidney 
L12: transplantation and remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality in kidney 
L13: transplant (KT) recipients, with a potential impact on graft survival. UTIs 
L14: after KT are usually caused by Gram-negative microorganisms. Other pathogens 
L15: which are uncommon in the general population should be considered in KT 
L16: patients, especially BK virus since an early diagnosis is necessary to improve 
L17: the prognosis. UTIs following kidney transplantation are classified into acute 
L18: simple cystitis, acute pyelonephritis/complicated UTI, and recurrent UTI, due to
L19:  their different clinical presentation, prognosis, and management. Asymptomatic 
L20: bacteriuria (ASB) represents a frequent finding after kidney transplantation, 
L21: but ASB is considered to be a separate entity apart from UTI since it is not 
L22: necessarily a disease state. In fact, current guidelines do not recommend 
L23: routine screening and treatment of ASB in KT patients, since a beneficial effect
L24:  has not been shown. Harmful effects such as the development of multidrug-
L25: resistant (MDR) bacteria and a higher incidence of Clostridium difficile

L27: Introduction Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are the most common infection in 
L28: kidney transplant (KT) patients, accounting for 42–75% of overall and 30% of all
L29:  hospitalizations for sepsis [1,2,3]. The prevalence of UTIs varies between the 
L30: series from 7 to 80%, due to the differences in definition, prophylactic 
L31: antibiotic regimens, geographical location, and follow-up periods [4]. A meta-
L32: analysis that included 13 studies with a total of 3364 patients, found a pooled 
L33: prevalence of UTIs of 38% with a range from 16 to 75%, and there were 
L34: significant differences between Americans and Europeans by subgroup analysis 
L35: (41% vs. 33%) and according to the follow-up time, being higher in patients 
L36: followed for 1–2 years than those followed for 2–5 years (34% vs. 43%) [5]. In 
L37: addition to this high incidence, UTIs in KT recipients are a major cause of 
L38: morbidity, hospitalization, and mortality, with impact on the patient’s well-
L39: being and associated with other complications such as, development of resistant 
L40: bacteria, drug interactions, and potential effects on graft survival. Therefore,
L41:  diagnosis, prevention, and management of UTI, as well as the understanding of 
L42: the special predisposition of these patients, are essential in the KT practice 
L43: in order to minimize their complications. This article reviews definitions, 
L44: etiology, clinical criteria, diagnosis and screening of UTIs in KTs, as well as 
L45: their risk factors and impact on graft survival. 2\. Risk Factors The risk 
L46: factors for UTIs in KT recipients are the same as in the general population, 
L47: such as female gender, elder age, pre-transplant urinary tract abnormalities, 
L48: diabetes mellitus, a history of recurrent UTIs or polycystic kidney disease [1].

[12] A Current Review of the Etiology, Clinical Features, and Diagnosis of Urinary Tract Infection in Renal Transplant Patients (https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4418/11/8/1456)
**viewing lines [211 - 290] of 941**

L211:  Diagnosis Diagnosis of an UTI is based on the presence of lower urinary tract 
L212: symptoms in cystitis (dysuria, urinary urgency or frequency or suprapubic pain) 
L213: or upper urinary tract symptoms in pyelonephritis or complicated UTI (fever, 
L214: chills, malaise, hemodynamic instability or allograft pain), and significant 
L215: quantitative count of bacteria in an appropriately collected urine specimen [2] 
L216: (Table 3). However, symptoms usually are masked due to immunosuppression and 
L217: surgical denervation of the kidney allograft and ureter, for example, urinary 
L218: symptoms and/or allograft pain cannot be present. Thus, the diagnosis should not
L219:  only be based on classical signs and symptoms, since the clinical features 
L220: frequently are not typical in this population. In fact, the first manifestation 
L221: of UTI may be isolated fever or even a non-specific sepsis syndrome. Associated 
L222: bacteremia is present in 3 to 16% of the cases of UTI [10,17], being more 
L223: frequent in the first months after transplantation. Acute kidney failure is 
L224: commonly observed in transplant pyelonephritis due to direct invasion of the 
L225: kidney parenchyma by the uropathogen, resulting in acute infectious 
L226: tubulointerstitial nephritis or associated with septic shock if it is present. 
L227: Urine analysis and urine culture are indicated if UTI is suspected, and blood 
L228: cultures should be collected in case of severe systemic symptoms. In case of 
L229: UTI, the urine dipstick is usually positive for nitrites, blood, protein, and 
L230: leukocyte esterase, and the urine microscopy typically shows pyuria, defined by 
L231: more than 10 white blood cells per milliliter (WBC/mL). Since the presence of 
L232: pyuria alone cannot be used to diagnose a UTI, other different diagnoses should 
L233: be considered in its absence. However, less than 10 WBC/mL in the urine may be 
L234: indicative of a UTI if typical symptoms or a consistent clinical context are 
L235: present. Bacteriuria is confirmed by a urine culture and allows for the 
L236: determination of antibiotic sensitivity in order to direct the treatment, even 
L237: retrospectively if the antibiotic has been started empirically. Bacteriuria is 
L238: defined as the presence of bacterial growth in urine and is considered 
L239: significant when it meets the standard quantitative criterion of greater than 
L240: 10⁵ CFU/mL, in order to rule out contamination of the sample. However, this 
L241: criterion varies according to the form of clinical presentation, 10³ CFU/mL for 
L242: cystitis and 10⁴ CFU/mL for acute pyelonephritis or complicated UTIs are 
L243: considered also significant growth [2]. It should be noted that the low CFU/mL 
L244: in cystitis are mainly limited to E. coli [48], whereas not all organisms found 
L245: in urine cultures are pathogens such as, Staphylococcus epidermidis (except in 
L246: the presence of ureteral stents), Lactobacillus, and Gardnerella vaginalis. The 
L247: urine can be contaminated during the collection of the sample by bacteria that 
L248: colonize the distal urethra and genital mucosa, so it is recommended to clean 
L249: the urinary meatus beforehand, collect the urine sample midstream in a sterile 
L250: container, and in case it is not taken immediately to the laboratory, store in a
L251:  refrigerator to avoid bacterial overgrowth. For the diagnosis of UTI, the 
L252: sample must be collected before starting the antibiotic treatment and straight 
L253: catheterization to obtain a urine specimen can be considered as an alternative. 
L254: Furthermore, catheter removal and collecting either during midstream urination 
L255: or via a newly placed catheter is recommended for patients with indwelling 
L256: catheters, especially those in place for more than 2 weeks, and a suspected 
L257: urinary tract infection [47]. The growth of multiple bacteria in a urine culture
L258:  may indicate contamination of the sample or an incorrect collection technique. 
L259: Screening of ASB in KT patients has been controversial due to the supposed risk 
L260: of progression to symptomatic UTI and the impact on graft survival. However, the
L261:  majority of studies have not found this association and at present, there is no
L262:  conclusive evidence that suggests screening for ASB and that its treatment 
L263: improve outcomes. In fact, a positive effect of colonizing bacteria has also 
L264: been proposed as in the general population, due to competition for nutrients or 
L265: receptor sites against other more virulent microorganisms or to the host’s 
L266: cross-protective immune or inflammatory response. Data suggest that ASB often 
L267: spontaneously resolves itself without antibiotics. Moreover, the treatment of 
L268: ASB has been associated with antibiotic harmful effects such as the development 
L269: of multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria, a higher incidence of Clostridium 
L270: difficile diarrhea, and increased healthcare costs [49]. Concern about ASB in 
L271: the first 1–3 months after transplantation has been raised due to higher 
L272: immunosuppression and surgical manipulation immediately post-transplant, 
L273: however, there is not enough evidence to support this [50]. Thus, recent 
L274: guidelines do not recommend routine screening and treatment of ASB in KT 
L275: patients [2,3,47], however, screening can be considered in the first 1–3 months 
L276: post-transplant, and treatment only if there have been two consecutive positive 
L277: urine cultures for the same bacteria. Treatment of ASB of multi-drug resistant 
L278: bacteria is not recommended. Nevertheless, treatment of persistent ASB can be 
L279: considered in patients with associated, unexplained, impaired renal function due
L280:  to the rare occurrence of asymptomatic pyelonephritis [2]. As in the general 
L281: population, screening of ASB is indicated in pregnant women and prior to 
L282: urological surgery, including before allograft biopsy, since in these cases, 
L283: treatment is mandatory [2,47]. Despite the above, most transplant centers 
L284: routinely screen for ASB. In addition to laboratory testing, renal ultrasound or
L285:  non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan should be considered to assess 
L286: complications such as obstruction and abscess, especially in patients with signs
L287:  of severe infection or those who do not fully respond to initial therapy [51].

Final assessment of microbiological tests needed for this patient:

Patient: Post-kidney transplant (12 days), immunosuppressed (tacrolimus, mycophenolate, post-thymoglobulin), CMV IgG negative recipient, with:
1. Dysuria with tachycardia (HR 128) - suggests UTI/possible urosepsis
2. Abnormal labs and diarrhea - requires infectious workup
3. Rising creatinine (1.1→1.3) - could be rejection or infection-related
4. Hematuria (22 RBCs), proteinuria, positive blood on dipstick
5. Ureteral stent in place (infection risk)

Necessary microbiological tests:

For UTI/Urosepsis workup (dysuria + tachycardia + stent):
1. URINE CULTURE - Standard for UTI diagnosis 【12†L227】
2. Blood Culture, Routine - For suspected urosepsis/bacteremia with tachycardia 【12†L228】

For post-transplant viral surveillance:
3. CMV Viral Load - CMV-negative recipient on immunosuppression; standard monitoring at 2 weeks post-transplant; also part of diarrhea workup 【7†L21-L27】

For diarrhea workup in immunosuppressed transplant patient:
4. CLOSTRIDIUM DIFFICILE TOXIN A & B TEST - Most common infectious cause of post-transplant diarrhea; patient on antibiotics (TMP-SMX, ciprofloxacin) 【7†L21】
5. FECAL CULTURE - Standard bacterial stool culture for diarrhea workup 【7†L28】

These 5 tests cover the main clinical concerns: UTI/sepsis, CMV monitoring, and infectious diarrhea workup.

- Chief complaint: Right arm pain (from triage data)

- Currently being managed with Enoxaparin, Warfarin, Trazodone, Docusate

- EDTA Hold specimen kept

**Key Findings**:
1. Right arm pain with venous duplex ultrasound → likely **upper extremity DVT** (deep vein thrombosis)
2. Being treated with Enoxaparin (therapeutic dose 100mg) and Warfarin → confirms anticoagulation for thrombosis
3. Blood parasite smear for malaria ordered → concern for tropical/infectious etiology
4. Lyme serology ordered → concern for tick-borne infection
5. Elevated neutrophils and ALT → mild systemic inflammation/infection

The clinical picture suggests: A young man presenting with right arm pain, concern for upper extremity DVT, AND concern for an infectious etiology (malaria and Lyme disease being worked up). The combination of blood parasite smear and Lyme serology suggests the clinicians are considering tick-borne or mosquito-borne infections, possibly with febrile illness and arm symptoms.

Given the already-ordered Lyme serology was negative and blood parasite smear was negative, the microbiological workup should encompass:
1. Already done: Lyme serology, Blood parasite smear
2. Likely needed: Blood cultures (for febrile workup), additional tick-borne disease testing (Babesia, Anaplasma, Ehrlichia), possibly viral serologies

L3: Group B Strep Infection: GBS Group B Streptococcus also known as Group B Strep 
L4: Infection (GBS) is a type of bacterial infection that can be found in a pregnant
L5:  woman’s vagina or rectum. This bacteria is normally found in the vagina and/or 
L6: rectum of about 25% of all healthy, adult women. Women who test positive for GBS
L7:  are said to be colonized. A mother can pass GBS to her baby during delivery. 
L8: GBS affects about 1 in every 2,000 babies in the United States. Not every baby 
L9: who is born to a mother who tests positive for GBS will become ill. Although GBS
L10:  is rare in pregnant women, the outcome can be severe. As such, physicians 
L11: include testing as a routine part of prenatal care. How can I find out if I have
L12:  Group B Strep infection? The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) 
L13: has recommended routine screening for vaginal strep B for all pregnant women. 
L14: This screening is performed between the 35th and 37th week of pregnancy. Studies
L15:  show that testing done within 5 weeks of delivery is the most accurate at 
L16: predicting the GBS status at birth. The test involves a swab of both the vagina 
L17: and the rectum. The sample is then taken to a lab where a culture is analyzed 
L18: for any presence of GBS. Test results are usually available within 24 to 48 
L19: hours. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that all women who have 
L20: risk factors PRIOR to being screened for GBS (for example, women who have 
L21: preterm labor beginning before completing 37 gestational weeks) are treated with
L22:  IV antibiotics until their GBS status is established. How does someone get 
L23: group B strep? Group B strep is not a sexually transmitted disease (STD). The 
L24: bacteria that causes group B strep normally lives in the intestines, vagina, or 
L25: rectum, and approximately 25% of all healthy women carry group B strep bacteria.
L26:  For most women, there are no symptoms of carrying the GBS bacteria. What if I 
L27: test positive for Group B Strep? If you test positive for GBS, this simply means
L28:  you are a carrier. Not every baby who is born to a mother who tests positive 
L29: for GBS will become ill. Approximately 1 out of every 200 babies whose mothers 
L30: carry GBS and are not treated with antibiotics will develop signs and symptoms 
L31: of GBS. There are, however, symptoms that may indicate you are at a higher risk 
L32: of delivering a baby with GBS. These symptoms include: * Labor or rupture of 
L33: membranes before 37 weeks * Rupture of membranes 18 hours or more before 
L34: delivery * Fever during labor * A urinary tract infection as a result of GBS 
L35: during your pregnancy * A previous baby with GBS In this case, your physician 
L36: will want to use antibiotics to protect your baby from contracting GBS during 
L37: delivery. According to the CDC, if you have tested positive and are not high 
L38: risk, your chances of delivering a baby with GBS are: * 1 in 200 if antibiotics 
L39: are not given * 1 in 4000 if antibiotics are given How can I protect my baby 
L40: from Group B Strep? If you test positive for GBS and meet the high-risk 
L41: criteria, your physician will probably recommend giving you antibiotics through 
L42: an IV during your delivery to prevent your baby from becoming ill. Taking 
L43: antibiotics greatly decreases the chances of your baby developing early-onset 
L44: group B strep infection. For women who are group B strep carriers, antibiotics 
L45: given before labor begins are not effective at preventing the transmission of 
L46: the group B bacteria. Since they naturally live in the gastrointestinal tract, 
L47: the bacteria can come back after taking antibiotics. A woman may test positive

L49: pregnant women to be tested for group B strep between 35 to 37 weeks of every

Now I have the complete list of 171 candidate microbiological tests. Let me determine which ones are necessary for this patient.

Patient: 39yo G1P0 at ~35 weeks with cervical cerclage, GBS+ by urine, uterine fibroids, presenting with STAT labs on May 5 (likely for evaluation of possible preterm labor or infection concern).

The microbiological tests that have been ordered already:
- May 5: URINE CULTURE (contaminated result)

Previously ordered at cerclage evaluation (Jan 25):
- URINE CULTURE
- Chlamydia trachomatis, Nucleic Acid Probe, with Amplification
- NEISSERIA GONORRHOEAE (GC), NUCLEIC ACID PROBE, WITH AMPLIFICATION
- SMEAR FOR BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS
- YEAST VAGINITIS CULTURE

Now, what tests are NECESSARY at this point (May 8, ~35 weeks)?

1. **URINE CULTURE** - Clearly needed. The May 5 culture was contaminated and needs to be repeated. UTI screening is essential in pregnancy, especially with a cerclage.

2. **R/O GROUP B BETA STREP** - Although ACOG says women with GBS bacteriuria don't need re-screening (they're considered colonized), this is still a commonly ordered test at 36-37 weeks. Since the patient is approaching that window, some providers might still order it. However, strictly speaking, it's NOT needed per guidelines.

3. **Chlamydia trachomatis, Nucleic Acid Probe, with Amplification** - Third trimester repeat STI screening. The CDC recommends retesting in the 3rd trimester for women <25 or at increased risk. While this patient is 39, having a cerclage could be considered a risk factor for adverse outcomes from STIs.

4. **NEISSERIA GONORRHOEAE (GC), NUCLEIC ACID PROBE, WITH AMPLIFICATION** - Same reasoning as Chlamydia.

5. **SMEAR FOR BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS** - BV screening is relevant given the cerclage, as BV is associated with preterm birth and ascending infection.

6. **YEAST VAGINITIS CULTURE** - Vaginal yeast infection screening.

Given the pattern from the patient's previous visit (where all of these were ordered together before cerclage), and the current clinical context of an urgent visit with a contaminated urine culture, the most necessary tests are:

1. URINE CULTURE (primary, needs repeat)
2. R/O GROUP B BETA STREP (approaching 36-37 week window, even if technically not needed per ACOG for GBS bacteriuria patients)
3. SMEAR FOR BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS (relevant with cerclage)
4. YEAST VAGINITIS CULTURE (vaginal screening)
5. Chlamydia trachomatis, Nucleic Acid Probe, with Amplification
6. NEISSERIA GONORRHOEAE (GC), NUCLEIC ACID PROBE, WITH AMPLIFICATION

Additional tests that may be necessary depending on clinical concern:
3. **SMEAR FOR BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS** - If concern about vaginal infection
4. **YEAST VAGINITIS CULTURE** - If vaginal symptoms

STI tests are less likely to be repeated in a 39-year-old married woman without risk factors.

I'll go with the tests that best match the clinical scenario. The urine culture is the clear primary test. Given the approaching delivery and need for prenatal screening completion, GBS screening and vaginal infection screening are also appropriate.

L2: Bipolar Disorders: Evaluation and Treatment Am Fam Physician. 
L3: 2021;103(4):227-239 Author disclosure: No relevant financial affiliations. 
L4: Bipolar disorders are common, recurrent mental health conditions of variable 
L5: severity that are difficult to diagnose. Affected individuals have higher rates 
L6: of other mental health disorders, substance use disorders, and comorbid chronic 
L7: medical illnesses. New diagnostic criteria and specifiers with attention on 
L8: mixed features and anxious distress aid the physician in recognizing episode 
L9: severity and prognosis. Physicians should consider bipolar disorder in any 
L10: patient presenting with depression. Pharmacotherapy with mood stabilizers, such 
L11: as lithium, anticonvulsants, and antipsychotics, is a first-line treatment that 
L12: should be continued indefinitely because of the risk of patient relapse. Active 
L13: lifestyle approaches include good nutrition, exercise, sleep hygiene, and proper
L14:  weight management. Monotherapy with antidepressants is contraindicated during 
L15: episodes with mixed features, manic episodes, and in bipolar I disorder. Ongoing
L16:  management involves monitoring for suicidal ideation, substance use disorders, 
L17: treatment adherence, and recognizing medical complications of pharmacotherapy. 
L18: Psychotherapy is a useful adjunct to pharmacotherapy. Patients and their support
L19:  systems should be educated about the chronic nature of this illness, possible 
L20: relapse, suicidality, environmental triggers (e.g., seasonal light changes, 
L21: shift work, other circadian disruption), and the effectiveness of early 
L22: intervention to reduce complications. Bipolar disorders comprise recurrent 
L23: episodes of elevated mood and depression.1 The relapse rate is more than 70% 
L24: over five years.2 Definitions of the various types of bipolar disorders are 
L25: provided in Table 13,4; diagnostic criteria are listed in Table 2.3 Hypomania 
L26: can occur in bipolar I and II disorders, whereas mania, which may include 
L27: psychosis, appears only in bipolar I disorder. The nature and prognosis of the 
L28: current episode and the likelihood of future ones can be described with specific
L29:  attributes3 (Table 33–5). Epidemiology Bipolar disorders, affecting more than 
L30: 1% of the world's population, have no predilection for race, sex, ethnicity, or 
L31: socioeconomic status.4 Bipolar I disorder has a higher lifetime incidence than 
L32: bipolar II disorder (0.6% and 0.4%, respectively).6 The mean age at onset is 18 
L33: years in bipolar I disorder and 22 years in bipolar II disorder.7 One-fourth of 
L34: patients presenting with depression or anxiety in a primary care setting have 
L35: been diagnosed with a bipolar disorder.8 Three-fourths of patients with bipolar 
L36: disorder have a history of three additional and concurrent mental health 
L37: conditions, most commonly anxiety disorders, impulse control and attention-
L38: deficit/hyperactivity disorders, and substance use disorders, which are 
L39: associated with worse outcomes.9,10 One-third of patients who have been 
L40: diagnosed with bipolar disorder will attempt suicide in their lifetime, 16% will
L41:  have attempted suicide within the past year, and 6% to 7% complete 
L42: suicide.11,12 Twenty-six percent of suicides occur within six weeks of a 
L43: hospital discharge.11,12 Patients who have anxious distress have a higher risk 
L44: of suicide, longer illness duration, and poorer response to medication.13 
L45: Etiology Bipolar disorders are multifactorial conditions with a genetic 
L46: predisposition affected by stress and the environment. Children of parents with 
L47: bipolar disorders have a 4% to 15% risk of being affected, compared with a less 
L48: than 2% risk in children of parents without bipolar disorder.12 Acute stressors 
L49: are often associated with the initial onset of illness and sometimes with 
L50: recurrence.5 These include stressful life events, adverse childhood events and 
L51: trauma, suicide of a family member, and disruptions in the sleep cycle.14 
L52: Biologic susceptibility, central and peripheral nervous system inflammation, 
L53: abnormal endocrine and neuronal pathways, and mitochondrial dysfunction 
L54: inheritance patterns have been implicated in bipolar disorders.15,16 Clinical 
L55: Presentation Patients typically present for treatment with depression or anxiety

L2: ATCDDD New search Hide text from Guidelines A ALIMENTARY TRACT AND METABOLISM 
L3: A11 VITAMINS Vitamins constitute a comprehensive group of therapeutic and 
L4: prophylactic preparations. Before classifying any product it is important to be 
L5: familiar with the main subdivision of the group. It may be necessary to consider
L6:  whether a product is a vitamin preparation with iron or an iron preparation 
L7: with vitamins, a mineral preparation with vitamins or a vitamin preparation with
L8:  minerals, or if the product should be regarded as a tonic etc. As an aid to 
L9: such considerations, guidelines are given at each sublevel. Vitamin B12 is 
L10: classified in B03 - Antianemic preparations. Vitamin K is classified in B02 - 
L11: Antihemorrhagics. Vitamins administered as i.v. solution additives, see B05XC. 
L12: Some definitions: Multivitamins: Products containing minimum vitamins A, B, C 
L13: and D. One B-vitamin is sufficient. B-complex: Products containing minimum 
L14: thiamine, riboflavine, pyridoxine, nicotinamide. The products may contain other 
L15: B-vitamins. Combinations of vitamins, vitamins with minerals or other substances
L16:  that do not belong to other 4th levels and are mainly indicated as food 
L17: supplements, see A11J. A11A MULTIVITAMINS, COMBINATIONS The DDDs are based on 
L18: prophylaxis. For simplicity, the DDDs for oral formulations are given as fixed 
L19: doses (1 tablet = 1 UD; 30 ml mixture = 6 UD). A11AA Multivitamins with minerals
L20:  The group is subdivided: A11AA01 - multivitamins and iron A11AA02 - 
L21: multivitamins and calcium A11AA03 - multivitamins and other minerals, incl. 
L22: combinations A11AA04 - multivitamins and trace elements In A11AA01, 02 and 03, 
L23: combinations with trace elements are allowed. In A11AA04 only trace elements are
L24:  allowed in addition to multivitamins. Combinations with other substances, e.g. 
L25: caffeine, are classified in A11AB. Cholin, biotin, inositol and para-amino 
L26: benzoic acid are regarded as vitamins and are allowed in preparations classified
L27:  in A11AA. A11AA01 multivitamins and iron Preparations containing multivitamins 
L28: and sub-therapeutic doses of iron are classified in this group. Sub-therapeutic 
L29: doses of iron are defined as 5-30 mg of Fe2+ per defined daily dose, with 
L30: corresponding limits for the various Fe3+ salts, if the main indication is not 
L31: "iron deficiency". Preparations containing more than 30 mg Fe2+ (or 
L32: corresponding doses of Fe3+) are classified as iron preparations (B03A) 
L33: regardless of therapeutic use. See also A11AA. A11AA02 multivitamins and calcium
L34:  Preparations containing multivitamins and sub-therapeutic doses of calcium are 
L35: classified in this group, e.g. a calcium content of up to 500 mg calcium 
L36: carbonate per tablet have been allowed. See also A11AA. Calcium preparations, 
L37: see A12A. A11AA03 multivitamins and other minerals, incl. combinations 
L38: Preparations containing multivitamins and sub-therapeutic doses of one or more 
L39: mineral are classified in this group. Definitions of sub-therapeutic doses of 
L40: iron and calcium, see A11AA01 and A11AA02. See also A11AA. Mineral supplements, 
L41: see A12. A11AA04 multivitamins and trace elements Preparations containing 
L42: multivitamins and trace elements are classified in this group. No other 
L43: combinations should occur in this group. A11AB Multivitamins, other combinations
L44:  This group comprises all combined preparations with multivitamins, which are 
L45: not classified in A11AA. Preparations containing caffeine etc. are classified in
L46:  this group. Preparations containing cholin, biotin, inositol, para-amino 
L47: benzoic acid etc. should be classified in A11AA. Last updated: 2026-01-20

L3: Bipolar Mania Treatment – Inpatient Psychiatry Today Author: Daniel Carlat M.D. 
L4: Last Updated: 4/1/20 Medicating Manic Episodes My Usual Approach The three key 
L5: medications we use to treat mania in the inpatient setting are antipsychotics, 
L6: mood stabilizers, and benzodiazepines. For patients who are very ill (meaning 
L7: agitated, very psychotic, and very dysfunctional), you might start with all 
L8: three. For others you might start more gingerly and monitor response. Generally 
L9: the most effective drugs for rapid control of acute mania are antipsychotics, 
L10: and combining them with mood stabilizers enhances their effectiveness. Which 
L11: antipsychotic should you start with? There are no clear head to head trials 
L12: showing that any particular antipsychotic is superior for mania. However, 
L13: clinical lore has it that olanzapine, quetiapine, and haloperidol are the 
L14: “bigger guns” and more effective in highly agitated and psychotic patients. 
L15: Unfortunately, all three of these are highly likely to cause side effects. My 
L16: philosophy is that I prefer to start with an anti-manic drug that will be most 
L17: tolerable for long term treatment. Given that philosophy, my first choice is 
L18: generally aripiprazole, and my second choice is usually risperidone. However, if
L19:  the patient is off-the-charts agitated and may become violent, I will start 
L20: with Zyprexa or Seroquel. I will also give an initial dose of a benzodiazepine, 
L21: because they work well and quickly and have few side effects. If you start with 
L22: aripiprazole or risperidone, both of which are higher potency antipsychotics, 
L23: you might worry about causing akathisia, which is a reasonable concern. But 
L24: since I’m prescribing Ativan as needed for anxiety, any really uncomfortable 
L25: akathisia will likely to be treated, at least initially, by the benzo. Later, if
L26:  I assess that akathisia is an ongoing problem, I’ll prescribe a standing dose 
L27: of propranolol and may discontinue the benzo altogether. Should you avoid using 
L28: benzo for mania in a substance user? While this is a matter of judgment, in 
L29: general I find the benefits for the short term treatment of mania outweigh any 
L30: risk of worsening substance use issues. I won’t plan on continuing the benzo for
L31:  more than a week, not long enough to cause tolerance. After a day or two of an 
L32: antipsychotic plus a benzodiazepine, I’ll re-evaluate, and if they are not 
L33: responding as well as I’d like, I’ll start a mood stabilizer, and my first 
L34: choice is lithium followed by depakote. What about carbamazepine (CBZ)? 
L35: Theoretically, it has the advantages over lithium and Depakote of causing less 
L36: weight gain. However, studies show that in the acute treatment of mania, 
L37: combining antipsychotics with CBZ doesn’t add any benefit, possibly because CBZ 
L38: revs up metabolic enzymes that may decrease serum levels of adjunct 
L39: antipsychotics. Using CBZ alone is fine, but you will usually reserve that for 
L40: treatment of less severe mania, or for maintenance treatment once the mania 
L41: subsides. Example of a common medication sequence for mania: Step One: Initial 
L42: dose of an antipsychotic and a benzodiazepine, followed by a standing daily dose
L43:  plus a prn dose of the benzo. Eg: Abilify 10 mg twice a day, first dose now. 
L44: Ativan 1 mg now, and thereafter 1 mg every 6 hours as needed for agitation. Step
L45:  Two (if no good response to above within two days): Lithobid 300 BID or 
L46: Eskalith CR 450 HS, increasing quickly to 900 HS. Prolonged release (PR) 
L47: versions of lithium are more tolerable, with less tremor, upper gastrointestinal
L48:  cramping, nausea, rash, cognitive dulling, urinary frequency. However,

18816093-RR-18   18816093        nan        RR       18 2130-05-09 09:57:00 2130-05-09 14:35:00 EXAMINATION:  MRCP\n\nINDICATION:  ___ year old woman with ruq pain X 4 weeks with radiation to the\nback. s/p CCX, on CT done elsewhere - 2 cm pancreas tail mass and mild PD\ndilation  // assess tail mass; pl also comment on possible causes of RUQ pain\n\nTECHNIQUE:  T1- and T2-weighted multiplanar images of the abdomen were\nacquired in a 1.5 T magnet.\nIntravenous contrast: 12 mL Gadavist.\nOral contrast:  1 cc of Gadavist mixed with 50 cc of water was administered\nfor oral contrast.\n\nCOMPARISON:  Compared to prior CT of the chest performed at outside hospital\ndated ___.\n\nFINDINGS: \n\nLower Thorax: Lung bases are clear.  No pleural or pericardial effusion.\n\nLiver: Liver demonstrates normal contours without morphological signs of liver\ncirrhosis.  There is diffuse drop of signal on the out of phase images as\ncompared to the inphase images compatible with mild hepatic steatosis.  The\nfat fraction measures 11%.  No worrisome enhancing hepatic mass lesions.\n\nBiliary: Status post cholecystectomy.  There is no intrahepatic biliary duct\ndilation.  Mild prominence of the extrahepatic biliary ducts, however within\nnormal limits of post cholecystectomy status.  The common bile duct tapers\nnormally towards the ampulla without obstructing filling defects or\ncholedocholithiasis.\n\nPancreas: There is a well-defined 3.5 x 3.5 x 3.6 cm partially exophytic soft\ntissue mass lesion arising from the pancreatic tail anteriorly that\ndemonstrates hyperintense signal on the T2 weighted images and hypointense\nsignal on the T1 weighted images.  There is avid homogeneous enhancement on\nthe postcontrast images and no surrounding inflammatory change.  The main\npancreatic duct is normal in caliber.  Normal pancreatic parenchyma surrounds\nthe lateral, medial and posterior aspects of the mass with preservation of the\nfat plane between the pancreatic tail and the splenic hilum.  The remainder of\nthe pancreas demonstrates normal signal intensity on T1 weighted images and\nenhances homogeneously.\n\nSpleen: Spleen is normal in size and signal characteristics.  There is a\nwell-defined 16 mm nodule within the inferolateral aspect of the spleen best\nseen on the arterial phase images (series 17, image 47) however becomes\nhomogeneous to the surrounding splenic parenchyma on the more delayed phases. \nIt demonstrates isointense signal to the spleen on all other imaging\nsequences.  No other splenic lesions identified.\n\nAdrenal Glands: 13 mm nodule within the left adrenal gland that demonstrates\ndrop signal on the out of phase images compatible with an adrenal adenoma. \nRight adrenal gland is normal.\n\nKidneys: The kidneys are symmetric in size bilaterally and demonstrate good\ncorticomedullary differentiation.  There is adequate excretion of contrast on\nthe more delayed phases.  No suspicious renal masses or hydronephrosis.\n\nGastrointestinal Tract:  The stomach, visualized small bowel and colon in the\nupper abdomen are within normal limits.  No ascites.\n\nLymph Nodes: No suspicious mesenteric, retroperitoneal or porta hepatis\nlymphadenopathy by size criteria.\n\nVasculature: Abdominal aorta is normal in caliber and its major branches are\npatent.  Hepatic arterial anatomy is conventional.  There is no splenic artery\npseudoaneurysm.  The splenic vein, SMV, portal vein and hepatic veins are\npatent.\n\nOsseous and Soft Tissue Structures: No suspicious osseous or soft mass\nlesions.\n\nIMPRESSION: \n\n1.  3.6 cm partially exophytic enhancing soft tissue mass lesion arising from\nthe pancreatic tail anteriorly compatible with the biopsy-proven\nneuroendocrine tumor.  There is preservation of the fat plane between the\npancreatic tail and splenic hilum.  The splenic artery and vein remain patent.\nNo peripancreatic lymph nodes.\n\n2.  Diffuse hepatic steatosis.  No worrisome enhancing hepatic mass lesions.\n\n3. 16 mm nodule within the inferolateral aspect of the spleen best seen on the\narterial phase images.  It demonstrates isointense signal to the background\nspleen on all other imaging sequences.  This most likely represents a splenic\nhamartoma.   A single metastatic lesion from a neuroendocrine tumor to the\nspleen would be unusual however not completely excluded.\n\n4.  13 mm left adrenal adenoma.\n

L3: Surgery for Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumor | American Cancer Society Two 
L4: general types of surgery can be used for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors 
L5: (pNETs): * Potentially curative surgery is used when the results of exams and 
L6: tests suggest that it’s possible to remove (resect) all the cancer. * Palliative
L7:  surgery may be done if imaging tests show that the cancer is too widespread to 
L8: be removed completely. This surgery is done to reduce tumor size to relieve 
L9: symptoms from excess hormone production or to prevent certain complications like
L10:  a blocked bile duct or intestine. The goal is not to try to cure the cancer. 
L11: This may also be called debulking surgery. Sometimes, however, after the surgeon
L12:  starts the operation, it becomes clear that the cancer has grown too far to be 
L13: completely taken out. If this happens, the operation may be stopped, or the 
L14: surgeon might continue with a smaller operation to help prevent or relieve 
L15: symptoms. Determining which pNETs can be surgically removed To know if the 
L16: cancer can be surgically removed, it is staged before the surgery, and 
L17: sometimes, during the surgery. Staging before surgery This uses imaging tests, 
L18: such as CT scans, MRI scans, and/or radionuclide scans, to see if the cancer has
L19:  spread beyond the pancreas, both locally and distantly. Exploratory laparoscopy
L20:  may also be done to help determine if the cancer has spread and if it can be 
L21: resected. For this procedure, the surgeon makes a few small incisions (cuts) in 
L22: the abdomen (belly) and inserts long, thin instruments. One instrument has a 
L23: small video camera on the end so the surgeon can see inside the abdomen. The 
L24: surgeon can look at the pancreas and other organs for tumors and take biopsy 
L25: samples of abnormal areas to learn how far the cancer has spread. Staging during
L26:  surgery Even after imaging tests are completed, the pancreas may still need to 
L27: be looked at closely to understand if the tumor can be removed safely. In these 
L28: cases, intraoperative imaging, such as an intraoperative ultrasound, will need 
L29: to be done. Intraoperative ultrasound is used during the surgery to better 
L30: understand structures near the pancreas tumor. Potentially curative surgery 
L31: PNETs that have not spread outside the pancreas should be completely removed, if
L32:  possible, because these tumors are more likely to be cured with surgery. Many 
L33: of these types of surgery are complex and can be very hard for patients. They 
L34: can cause complications and can take weeks or months to make a full recovery. If
L35:  you're thinking about having this type of surgery, it’s important to weigh the 
L36: benefits and risks carefully. Types of potentially curative surgery include: * 
L37: Enucleation (removing only the tumor) * Central pancreatectomy * Distal 
L38: pancreatectomy * Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) * Total 
L39: pancreatectomy The type of surgery needed depends on several factors, including 
L40: the location, size, and specific kind of pNET (functioning or non-functioning). 
L41: Enucleation (removing just the tumor) Sometimes if a pNET is small, just the 
L42: tumor itself is removed. This is called enucleation. This operation may be done 
L43: using a laparoscope, so that only a few small cuts on the belly are needed. This
L44:  surgery may be an option for patients with an insulinoma or a gastrinoma 
L45: smaller than 2 cm (less than 1 inch), since these pNETs are thought to be less 
L46: aggressive. For pNETs that are located close to the common bile duct or 
L47: pancreatic duct, are larger than 3 cm (a little more than an inch), and are 
L48: suspected of having spread to nearby lymph nodes, enucleation is commonly not 
L49: the first surgical approach. Central pancreatectomy A central pancreatectomy is 
L50: a surgical option for small, low-grade pNETs in the neck or upper body of the 
L51: pancreas, if enucleation cannot be done safely. The surgeon removes only the

L51: pancreas, if enucleation cannot be done safely. The surgeon removes only the 
L52: neck and upper body of the pancreas, keeping the pancreatic head and tail 
L53: intact. This helps keep most functions of the pancreas. Distal pancreatectomy A 
L54: distal pancreatectomy is used to treat pNETs in the tail and body of the 
L55: pancreas. Surgery removes only the tail of the pancreas or the tail and part of 
L56: the body of the pancreas. The spleen is usually removed as well, but it can be 
L57: saved in certain situations. The spleen helps the body fight infections, so if 
L58: it’s removed, you’ll be at increased risk for infection with certain bacteria. 
L59: To help with this, doctors recommend that patients get certain vaccines before 
L60: having this surgery. Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) A Whipple 
L61: procedure treats pNETs found in the head of the pancreas that cannot be removed 
L62: by enucleation. During this operation, the surgeon removes the head of the 
L63: pancreas and sometimes the body of the pancreas as well. Nearby structures such 
L64: as part of the small intestine (duodenum), part of the bile duct, the 
L65: gallbladder, lymph nodes near the pancreas, and sometimes part of the stomach 
L66: are also removed. The remaining bile duct and pancreas are then attached to the 
L67: small intestine so that bile and digestive enzymes can still go into the small 
L68: intestine. The small intestine (or the stomach and small intestine) is then 
L69: reattached so that food can pass through the digestive tract. Most often, this 
L70: operation is done through a large incision (cut) down the middle of the belly. 
L71: Some doctors at major cancer centers also do the operation laparoscopically, 
L72: which is sometimes known as keyhole surgery. This is a very complex surgery that
L73:  requires a lot of skill and experience. It carries a relatively high risk of 
L74: complications that can be life- threatening. When the operation is done in small
L75:  hospitals or by doctors with less experience, as many as 15% of patients may 
L76: die as a result of surgical complications. In contrast, when the operation is 
L77: done in cancer centers by surgeons experienced in the procedure, less than 5% of
L78:  patients die as a direct result of surgery. In general, people having this type
L79:  of surgery do better at a hospital that does at least 15 to 20 Whipple 
L80: procedures per year. Still, even under the best circumstances, many patients 
L81: have complications from the surgery. These can include: * Leaking from the 
L82: various connections between organs that the surgeon has joined * Infections * 
L83: Bleeding * Trouble with the stomach emptying after eating * Trouble digesting 
L84: some foods (which might require taking pancreatic enzymes in pill form to help 
L85: with digestion) * Weight loss * Changes in bowel habits * Diabetes Total 
L86: pancreatectomy Total pancreatectomy might be an option if the cancer has spread 
L87: throughout the pancreas but can still be removed. This operation removes the 
L88: entire pancreas, as well as the gallbladder, part of the stomach and small 
L89: intestine, and the spleen. But this type of surgery is used less often than the 
L90: other operations because there doesn’t seem to be a major advantage in removing 
L91: the whole pancreas, and it can have major side effects. It’s possible to live 
L92: without a pancreas. But when the entire pancreas is removed, people are left 
L93: without the cells that make insulin and other hormones that help maintain safe 
L94: blood sugar levels. These people develop diabetes, which can be hard to manage 
L95: because they are totally dependent on insulin shots. People who have had this 
L96: surgery also need to take pancreatic enzyme pills to help them digest certain 
L97: foods. Before this operation, your doctor will recommend that you get certain 
L98: vaccines because your spleen (which has an important role in your immune system)
L99:  will be removed. Palliative surgery for pNETs If the cancer has spread too far 
L100: to be removed completely, any surgery being considered would be palliative 
L101: (intended to relieve symptoms and improve your quality of life). This type of 
L102: surgery may be considered in some people with pNETs whose tumor has recurred and
L103:  is causing local problems or is making too many hormones that are causing

L0:

L2: Use of ERCP in the United States over the past decade Show available content in 
L3: Introduction Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is a complex 
L4: endoscopic procedure used to evaluate pancreatobiliary ductal anatomy through 
L5: the use of fluoroscopy and contrast to determine suitable interventions for both
L6:  benign and malignant pathology. ERCP was initially developed in the late 1960’s
L7:  as a diagnostic procedure and subsequently evolved to a therapeutic procedure 
L8: with the first biliary sphincterotomy performed in 1974 in Kyoto, Japan 1 2 3 4 
L9: . In recent years, the role of ERCP has shifted from being a diagnostic and 
L10: therapeutic procedure, to mainly being a therapeutic procedure 5 . Previous 
L11: reports have shown that inpatient utilization of ERCP has been decreasing since 
L12: 1996, which is believed to be due to the widespread availability of newer 
L13: imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) 
L14: and endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) 5 6 7 8 . In the United States, current training
L15:  in ERCP requires a prior 3-year training in internal medicine followed by a 
L16: 3-year training program in general gastroenterology and finally an additional 
L17: year in advanced endoscopy training. During that final year, the trainee is 
L18: expected to acquire the necessary cognitive skills for decision-making, as well 
L19: as the core ERCP technical skills 9 10 . As the demand for advanced endoscopists
L20:  continues to increase, the number of academic programs offering ERCP training 
L21: has increased, which highlights the importance of competency assessment in the 
L22: area 10 11 . Some of the key factors that have been noted to influence 
L23: competency positively include training at large-volume centers and a bile duct 
L24: cannulation rate of 80 % to 90 %, emphasizing that the total number of 
L25: procedures to achieve proficiency varies among trainees and should, as such, be 
L26: individualized 12 13 14 15 16 . Although previous epidemiological data are 
L27: available on the topic, there have been significant recent technological and 
L28: scientific advances in advanced endoscopy. There continues to be a paucity of 
L29: recent large studies exploring temporal trends in the use of ERCP. Thus, the aim
L30:  of the current study was to assess the current temporal trends in inpatient 
L31: utilization of ERCP, and identification of common indications and interventions,
L32:  procedural complications, and healthcare resource utilization using the largest
L33:  public inpatient database in the United States throughout the past decade. 
L34: Patients and methods Study design and data source Patients were selected from 
L35: the Nationwide Inpatient Sample (NIS) which is the largest publicly available, 
L36: inpatient, all-payer database in the United States. The dataset for the years 
L37: 2007 to 2016 contains more than 70 million hospital stays, which are a 20 % 
L38: stratified sample of over 4,000 non-federal acute care hospitals of more than 40
L39:  states of the United States, and is representative of 95 % of hospital 
L40: discharges nationwide. A principal diagnosis, defined as the primary discharge 
L41: diagnosis, as well as up to 29 other secondary diagnoses are included in the 
L42: dataset. The dataset also includes codes for up to 15 procedures performed 
L43: during the hospital stay. It also allows determining length of hospital stay, 
L44: and total hospitalization charges, as well as desired outcome measures such as 
L45: calculations of inpatient disease prevalence. All analyzed data was extracted 
L46: from the databases for the years 2007 to 2016 to design this retrospective 
L47: cohort study. Study population All patients in the NIS dataset for 2007 to 2016 
L48: with an International Classification of Diseases, Ninth and Tenth Revisions, 
L49: Clinical Modification (ICD-9 and ICD-10 CM) principal procedural code for ERCP 
L50: were identified, signifying that only all patients undergoing inpatient ERCP 
L51: were included. All codes are included in Supplemental Table 1 . In all patients 
L52: with an associated procedural code for ERCP, procedural specifics were obtained 
L53: using their respective procedural ICD-9/10 codes. These included biliary

L36: APPENDICES FOR: REPORT TO CONGRESS: SOCIAL RISK FACTORS AND PERFORMANCE UNDER 
L37: MEDICARE'S VALUE-BASED PURCHASING PROGRAMS � 3 Appendix for Executive Summary: 
L38: Summary of Program Findings, Strategies, and Considerations The executive 
L39: summary chapter of this report discusses the overall findings and considerations
L40:  across the nine programs evaluated. Those overall findings arose from analyses 
L41: that were conducted separately for each program and led to the formation of the 
L42: three strategies and their corresponding considerations presented in the 
L43: executive summary. However, each of these considerations applies somewhat 
L44: differently to each program, depending on their applicability and the program 
L45: structure. Additionally, some programs have considerations that are so program-
L46: specific that they do not fit into the three-strategy framework that applies 
L47: across programs. For example, for the Hospital Acquired Condition Reduction 
L48: Program (HACRP), the department recommends that the HACRP be updated with AHRQ's
L49:  revised PSI-90 measure. A summary of the research questions, findings, and 
L50: considerations are presented below. Each program's chapter in the full report 
L51: provides additional detail on the findings and considerations. I. The Hospital 
L52: Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP) Research Questions Is there a relationship
L53:  between beneficiary social risk and readmission rates? Is there a relationship 
L54: between hospital social risk profile and readmission rates? Are hospitals that 
L55: serve a high proportion of beneficiaries with social risk factors more likely to
L56:  receive penalties under the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program? How would 
L57: potential policy options to address issues of social risk and performance in the
L58:  Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program affect program penalties? Key Findings:
L59:  Underlying Relationships Dually-enrolled beneficiaries had significantly 
L60: greater odds of readmission than non-dually enrolled beneficiaries even within 
L61: the same hospitals, an effect that was relatively similar across hospitals 
L62: participating in the HRRP. APPENDICES FOR: REPORT TO CONGRESS: SOCIAL RISK 
L63: FACTORS AND PERFORMANCE UNDER MEDICARE'S VALUE-BASED PURCHASING PROGRAMS

L66: patient characteristics, provide poorer-quality care to prevent readmissions, or
